query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In face-centered-cubic (fcc) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni family, the retention of high fracture toughness is governed primarily by the degree of nanoscale chemical short-range order (SRO) because SRO lowers the intrinsic stacking-fault energy (SFE). A lower SFE stabilises partial-dislocation glide and deformation twinning/ε-martensite formation, which elevate strain-hardening and delay crack-tip localisation, thereby preserving toughness. Conversely, thermally disrupting the SRO raises the SFE, suppresses these auxiliary deformation modes, and reduces toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy produced by vacuum induction melting, homogenised at 1200 °C for 12 h and water-quenched to give a single-phase fcc solid solution with moderate baseline SRO from the quench.
generation.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment aimed solely at the SRO: (1) 800 °C anneal for 24 h followed by water quench (promotes and freezes in stronger SRO), versus (2) 1200 °C anneal for 1 h followed by water quench (destroys SRO and yields a nearly random solid solution). No compositional change or grain-growth allowed (grain size held ~10 µm by prior cold working and identical recrystallisation schedules).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical testing after heat treatment; identical grain size, texture and impurity content; fcc single-phase stability (no precipitation).
generation.structural_mediator: Magnitude of chemical short-range order, quantified by Warren–Cowley parameters (α_1 nearest-neighbour values) from synchrotron diffuse-scattering and by the planar fault probability measured in high-resolution TEM.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced SRO locally lowers the SFE (~10–20 mJ m⁻² drop) because energetically favourable unlike-atom nearest-neighbour pairs stabilise hcp-like stacking. Lower SFE facilitates dissociation of perfect dislocations into widely separated Shockley partials and promotes deformation twinning or ε-martensite formation at the crack tip. These auxiliary deformation modes raise the work-hardening exponent, spread plasticity, blunt the crack and therefore increase fracture toughness. When SRO is eliminated, the SFE rises, twinning/TRIP are suppressed, strain hardening is lower, and cracks localise sooner, reducing toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome:
Relative to the baseline (low-SRO, high-temperature-homogenised state):
• The 800 °C/24 h SRO-enriched condition will show (i) ≈30-50 % larger plastic-zone size at a given K, (ii) ≥25 % higher ASTM-E399 plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC (e.g., rising from ~170 MPa√m to ≥210 MPa√m), (iii) pronounced deformation twins/ε-hcp plates near the fracture surface, and (iv) lower experimentally determined SFE by at least 10 mJ m⁻².
• Charpy V-notch energy and tensile uniform elongation will rise proportionally.
• No significant change in elastic modulus or yield strength attributable solely to SRO.
generation.baseline: Same alloy in the high-temperature (1200 °C/1 h) homogenised, random-solution state with minimal SRO, tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis is expected to hold for single-phase fcc HEAs containing 40–70 at.% combined (Ni+Co) and 10–20 at.% Cr, with room-temperature SFE between ~10 and 45 mJ m⁻². It is not expected to apply to bcc HEAs, to fcc HEAs with SFE >50 mJ m⁻² (e.g., high-Al variants), or to temperatures above ~600 °C where diffusion eliminates SRO during testing.
generation.uncertainty: Direct, quantitative links between measured SRO, SFE and toughness in HEAs remain sparse; grain-boundary segregation or incipient precipitation during low-temperature anneal could complicate interpretation. Predicted magnitude (25–50 % toughness change) is therefore moderately uncertain (±15 %).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three specimen sets with identical grain size: (A) as-cast + 1200 °C/1 h quench (minimal SRO), (B) 800 °C/24 h quench (strong SRO), (C) same as B but followed by a brief 1050 °C/30 s flash anneal and immediate quench (destroys SRO without allowing grain growth). Measure SRO by synchrotron diffuse scattering (extract α_1), measure SFE by TEM weak-beam evaluation of partial‐dislocation spacing, and determine fracture toughness K_IC per ASTM E399 at 298 K.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If sets A, B and C show no systematic correlation between (α_1 or SFE) and fracture toughness, or if higher SRO (lower SFE) fails to raise toughness by at least 10 %, the hypothesis is falsified.
